newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-ANZ calls for merger freedom for banks.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-ANZ calls for merger freedom for banks.

text.p: The Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd called on Tuesday for the end of a government freeze on mergers between Australia's six biggest financial institutions and for a review of policy on foreign takeovers of local banks.

ANZ executive director Alister Maitland, outlining the bank's submission to the Wallis inquiry into the financial system, also called for even application of competition policy for the banking sector and for Australia's central bank to withdraw from commercial activities.

Also, in a departure from calls by life offices and rival National Australia Bank Ltd for a "super regulator" to oversee all financial intermediaries, ANZ called for the Reserve Bank to oversee banks and other deposit-takers separately.

"ANZ welcomes changes to the structure of regulation which will give flexibility in the way institutions position themselves to meet the challenges of all the markets in which they compete," ANZ chief executive Don Mercer said in a statement.
The Wallis inquiry, chaired by former Amcor Ltd chief Stan Wallis, is due to release a discussion paper in late November and make recommendations to the government in March.
ANZ's submission advocated the abolition of the so-called "six pillars" policy, which has frozen mergers between the nation's four major banks and two biggest life offices.
ANZ general manager of group regulatory affairs Sue McCarthy told a news conference that the bank did not want the "six pillars" policy scrapped because ANZ would benefit substantially from a merger.
"It's largely because we don't see any case for the rules on banking being any different from the rules on any other industry," McCarthy said.
ANZ also urged a clarification of official policy on takeovers of local banks by foreign banks, citing concern that head-office bank operations could be relocated offshore.

Under existing restrictions, the treasurer must approve any one shareholder holding over 10 percent of the voting stock of a bank. The treasurer must approve any one foreigner holding 15 percent and over of a company, and any aggregate foreign shareholding of 40 percent and above.
"If a bank or financial institution which already has a very wide shareholding wanted to take over an Australian bank, that's not necessarily caught up by those rules," ANZ's McCarthy said.

On the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), ANZ's submission called for the RBA to cease providing financial payments services, adding the cetral bank handled about half of all bulk electronic transactions exchanged among financial institutions.
"Because the RBA competes with banks for this business, it compromises its role of bank supervisor," the subbmission says.
